title: How to Choose Between Roth and Traditional 401(k) for Retirement
description: The 'Tax Bracket Bet' explained for employees.
content:
Most 401(k) plans now offer two doors: the Traditional 401(k) (Pre-Tax) and the Roth 401(k) (Post-Tax). The decision of which door to walk through determines whether you pay taxes today or pay taxes in 30 years. There is no universal right answer; it depends on your current tax bracket versus your expected bracket in retirement. This guide helps you place your bet based on your career stage and income trajectory.

Key Takeaways

  • The Low Earner Rule: If you are early in your career (low tax bracket), choose Roth. Pay the cheap taxes now to lock in tax-free growth on the huge compound interest ahead.
  • The High Earner Rule: If you are in your peak earning years (32% bracket), choose Traditional. You desperately need the tax deduction now. You will likely be in a lower bracket in retirement.
  • The 'Unknown' Hedge: Since we don't know future tax laws, splitting contributions 50/50 is a valid way to diversify 'Regulatory Risk'.
  • RMD Protection: Roth 401(k)s no longer have RMDs (starting 2024). Traditional 401(k)s force you to withdraw at age 73. Roth gives you more control.

Why It Matters (US Context)

Employer matches are almost always 'Pre-Tax' (Traditional). Even if you contribute 100% to Roth, your 4% match goes into the Traditional bucket. This naturally creates some tax diversification in your account.

The Decision Matrix

Find your zone.

Zone 1: Current Tax Rate < 22%

Verdict: Roth 401(k).
You are paying very little tax. Don't take a deduction you don't need. Lock in tax-free growth.

Zone 2: Current Tax Rate > 32%

Verdict: Traditional 401(k).
Saving $23,000 saves you ~$8,000 in taxes today. You can invest that tax savings. In retirement, you can fill up the lower brackets (10%, 12%) with withdrawals.

Zone 3: The 'Super Saver'

If you max out the $23,000 limit, the Roth allows you to effectively save more.
$23k in a Roth is worth more than $23k in a Traditional (because the Traditional still owes taxes).
Strategy: If you have excess cash flow, Roth packs more value into the contribution limit.

Tactical Considerations

  1. State Taxes: If you live in a high-tax state (CA/NY) now but plan to retire in a no-tax state (FL/TX), Traditional is a slam dunk. Dodge the 10% state tax today; pay 0% later.
  2. Early Retirees: Roth contributions (not earnings) can be rolled to a Roth IRA and accessed penalty-free after 5 years. This makes Roth 401(k) useful for the 'Bridge Period'.
  3. The 'Tax Torpedo': Traditional withdrawals count as income, which can make your Social Security taxable. Roth withdrawals do not. Having a big Roth bucket lowers your 'Provisional Income' in retirement.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I switch?

Yes. You can change your election at any time. You might do Roth in your 20s, Traditional in your 40s, and back to Roth in your 60s (part-time work).

Can I convert Traditional to Roth?

Yes, but you pay the tax bill immediately. This is best done in a low-income year (e.g., if you are laid off or take a sabbatical).

Do all employers offer Roth?

Most large ones do. If yours doesn't, stick to Traditional 401(k) and do your Roth saving in an IRA.
